title: Hallmarks, oncogenes and suppressors
summary: The hallmarks of cancer as an organising heuristic; accelerators and brakes; Knudson's two-hit model as a Poisson calculation; drivers and passengers.

shots.title:
What makes
a cancer.
shots.subtitle: Six capabilities, then more — a heuristic, not a law.
shots.narration: What does a normal cell have to acquire to become a cancer? The most cited answer is a list of capabilities called the hallmarks of cancer.
Hanahan and Weinberg proposed six hallmarks in 2000. In 2011 they added two more and two enabling characteristics. In 2022 Hanahan proposed further dimensions.

shots.heading: The original six (2000)
shots.narration: The original six: keep the growth signal on, ignore the brakes, refuse to die, divide without limit, recruit blood vessels, and invade other tissues.

shots.heading: Added in 2011
items: Context: the recruited normal cells of the **tumour microenvironment**
shots.narration: The 2011 update added reprogrammed metabolism and immune evasion as hallmarks, genome instability and inflammation as enabling characteristics, and the tumour microenvironment as context.

shots.text: Reprogrammed metabolism: many tumours **ferment glucose to lactate even with oxygen** — the Warburg effect.
shots.narration: One example: many tumours take up glucose and ferment it to lactate even when oxygen is available. One explanation is that dividing cells need carbon for building material, not just energy.

shots.text: Hanahan calls the scheme **provisional** — a way to organise complexity, not a physical law.
shots.narration: Treat the hallmarks as Hanahan himself does: a provisional heuristic for organising complexity, not a law of nature. Useful for framing a paper; not a model you can fit.
Two kinds of gene matter most. Oncogenes are accelerators: one activating mutation can be enough. Tumour suppressors are brakes: usually both copies must be lost before the brake fails.

notes: so about 5% of carriers get none
shots.narration: In 1971 Knudson studied forty-eight cases of a childhood eye cancer. If carriers average three tumours, Poisson statistics say about five percent get none — explaining carriers who stay healthy.

shots.text: Inherited form: one hit **inherited**, one acquired. Sporadic form: **both** hits acquired in the same cell lineage.
shots.narration: His explanation: the cancer needs two mutational hits. In the inherited form, one hit is inherited and the second occurs in a body cell. In the sporadic form, both occur by chance in body cells.

shots.text: A typical tumour carries **two to eight** driver mutations. Most of its other mutations are **passengers**.
shots.narration: Most of a tumour's mutations do nothing. A typical tumour carries two to eight driver mutations, in genes like these, among many passengers. Telling them apart is a statistics problem.

steps.title: Hallmark, enabler, or neither?
steps.brief: Hanahan and Weinberg distinguish hallmark capabilities from the enabling characteristics that help a tumour acquire them. Sort each item.

questions.prompt: A tumour-suppressor gene usually contributes to cancer when…
options: one copy gains a mutation that activates it
both copies are lost or inactivated
questions.explain: Brakes fail when both copies are gone — Knudson's two hits.

questions.prompt: How many driver mutations does a typical tumour carry, according to Vogelstein et al. (2013)?
questions.explain: Two to eight drivers; the many other mutations are passengers.

questions.prompt: How does Hanahan (2022) describe the hallmarks scheme?
options: As a complete mechanistic model of cancer
As a provisional heuristic for distilling complexity
questions.explain: A provisional organising framework — useful for structure, not for prediction.

questions.prompt: Carriers develop on average m = 3 tumours (Poisson). What percentage of carriers develop no tumour at all? (one decimal)
Same model: what percentage of carriers develop exactly one tumour?
Now suppose tumours fall independently in each eye, with mean 1.5 per eye. What percentage of carriers have tumours in both eyes?
questions.explain: P(an eye has at least one) = 1 − e^(−1.5) ≈ 0.777; both eyes: 0.777² ≈ 0.604. Bilateral tumours in carriers are exactly what Knudson's model explains.

questions.prompt: And what percentage have tumours in exactly one eye?
questions.explain: 2 × 0.777 × 0.223 ≈ 0.347. The three cases (none, one eye, both) sum to 100%.

steps.title: Homework 2 · Hallmarks as research questions
steps.brief: About 40 minutes. Short, precise answers beat long ones.

fields.label: 1. Show your working for the problem set: derive P(none), P(one eye) and P(both eyes) for the two-eye Poisson model, and explain what a different mean (say m = 1) would predict.
2. Pick one hallmark. Propose a computational question about it where a quantum method could plausibly help — then argue the opposite case as a sceptical referee would.
fields.hint: Chemistry of a target in that pathway? An optimisation over interacting genes? Be concrete about what is computed.

fields.label: 3. Drivers versus passengers is a statistics problem. In one paragraph, say what null model you would need to call a gene a driver, and why getting it wrong produces false positives.
